n: The bride wishes she could show affection to her beloved in public as freely as a sister could to a brother, without anyone frowning at her.
She would bring him home to her mother’s house — where she was taught — and share spiced wine with him.
She longs for his tender embrace, repeating an earlier line.
The refrain one last time: do not awaken love before its time. The book teaches patience and purity in love.

f.r: Song of Solomon 2:7; Song of Solomon 3:5

n: Onlookers see the couple coming from the wilderness, the bride leaning on her husband. She recalls where their love began, under the apple tree near the place he was born.

f.g: A picture of trust and dependence in marriage.

n: The book’s climax: she asks to be pressed on his heart and arm like a seal — a sign of belonging. True love is as strong as death, and its devotion burns like a fierce flame.

f.g: A signet stamp worn on a cord or ring, marking ownership and identity.
Possibly “the flame of the LORD” (Hebrew shalhebetyah) — the only hint of God’s name in the book.

n: No flood can put out true love, and no amount of wealth can buy it. Anyone who tried would be scorned. Love is a gift, not a purchase.
Her brothers speak about their young sister who is not yet grown: how should they protect her until someone asks to marry her?
If she is a “wall” — chaste and firm — they will honor her with silver. If she is a “door” — too open — they will protect her with cedar boards.

f.g: A symbol of virtue that resists advances.
A symbol of openness that needs guarding.

n: The bride declares that she was a “wall” — she kept herself pure — and so she found peace and favor in her husband’s eyes.

f.g: Literally “found peace” (shalom), perhaps a play on Solomon’s name.

n: Solomon owned a huge vineyard that he rented out to tenants, each paying a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.

f.g: A place name meaning “lord of a multitude”; its location is unknown.

n: But the bride’s own “vineyard” — herself — is hers to give. Solomon can keep his thousand pieces; her love is not for sale.
The groom asks to hear her voice, for his friends are listening and he longs to hear her speak.

f.g: The bride, at home in the gardens of love.

n: The bride’s final words: come quickly, my beloved, like a gazelle on spice-covered hills. The song ends with love still longing and alive.
